c: A fruit salad is a mixture — you can pick the pieces apart. A cake is a compound — you can’t get the eggs back.
A stadium: the nucleus is a pea on the center spot, electrons are flies in the stands. Isotopes are the same car model with different weight in the trunk.
A hotel: lower floors (shells) fill first, and each room (orbital) takes at most two guests.
A city map: the group is the street (neighbors with the same habits), the period is the floor of the building.
Ionic: one person hands a coin to another and they stick like magnets. Covalent: two people share one umbrella. Metallic: a crowd under one big blanket of electrons.
Valence is the number of hands an atom has; a correct formula is everyone holding hands with no hand left free.
Like surnames: “-at” and “-it” tell you the family the way “-ić” tells you a surname is Serbian.
A recipe and a bank statement at once: every atom that goes in must come out — nothing disappears.
Review week after the holidays — redo your error log and every flashcard you still miss.
A mole is a “chemist’s dozen”: you buy eggs by the tray and count atoms by 6.022·10²³.
Iron ore is a bag of mixed nuts: how many grams of the bag are cashews (Fe)?
A pancake recipe: 2 eggs per cup of flour. Make ten times more and the ratio stays the same.
Sandwiches with 10 slices of bread and 3 slices of cheese: the cheese runs out first and limits you.
Every mole of any gas takes the same parking space at STP — 22.4 L — whether it’s a small car (H₂) or a truck (CO₂).
Syrup in water: adding water doesn’t remove sugar, it spreads it out — so c₁V₁ = c₂V₂.
Salt in water is a dancing couple who split up the moment the music (water) starts.
pH works like the Richter scale: each step is ×10, so pH 3 is ten times more acidic than pH 4.
The stronger parent wins the argument: strong acid + weak base gives an acidic salt solution.
Electrons are money: oxidation loses money, reduction gains it. Rust is iron paying oxygen.
Le Chatelier is a seesaw: push one side and the system leans back to rebalance.
Metali: Na, Ca, Fe, Al, Cu
Group 1 metals are people desperate to give away one coin — so eager they react with plain water.
Nemetali: C, Si, N, S; karbonati, silikati
Silicate minerals are Lego: the same SiO₄ brick builds chains, sheets and 3D frames.
Like a dress rehearsal before opening night: the mistakes you find now cost nothing.
A carbon chain is a train: the longest track gives the name, branches are carriages on side tracks.
Isomers are anagrams: the same letters (atoms) make different words (molecules).
−OH is a handle that water can grab — that’s why ethanol mixes with water and oil doesn’t.
The same C=O badge: worn at the end of the chain it’s an aldehyde, in the middle it’s a ketone.
Esterification is a handshake between an acid and an alcohol that drops one water molecule; polymers and proteins are chains of repeating beads.
Exam training — timed, phone away, exam rules.
Exam training, then taper like before a race: keep it sharp and sleep well. The day before exam week is a rest day.
m: Negative numbers are debt: taking away a debt (− (−5)) is the same as getting money.
NZS is when two buses, one every 4 and one every 6 minutes, arrive together again (12 min).
Pizza slices: before adding, cut both pizzas into slices of the same size (common denominator).
+20% then −20% isn’t a return to start: the second 20% is taken from a bigger number.
Fold a paper in half again and again — its thickness goes 2, 4, 8, 16… that’s 2ⁿ.
Sorting fruit: you can only add apples to apples — x² terms with x² terms.
A square garden enlarged on two sides: the new area is a² + two strips ab + a small square b².
A balance scale: whatever you do to one side, do to the other and it stays level.
Two clues in a riddle: each alone isn’t enough, together they pin down the answer.
A ladder against a wall is Pythagoras; volume is how much water a container holds.
Like reducing 6/8 to 3/4 — you may cancel factors, never terms joined by + or −.
A taxi fare: a start fee (n) plus a fixed price per km (k) — y = kx + n.
The discriminant is a forecast: positive means two solutions, zero one, negative none.
The path of a thrown ball: the vertex is the highest point it reaches.
Absolute value is distance: 3 km left or right of home is still 3 km.
Bacteria doubling every hour, or savings with compound interest.
The log asks “how many times did I multiply?” — the pH and Richter scales are logarithms.
A Ferris wheel: your height above the center is sin, your sideways position is cos.
Same person, different outfits: sin²x + cos²x is always 1, however it’s dressed.
Planimetrija: sličnost, sinusna i kosinusna teorema
Similarity is a photo enlargement; surveyors use the sine theorem to measure across a river.
Three cone-shaped cups of water fill a cylinder with the same base and height — so V(cone) = V/3.
Review week — redo your error log.
Arithmetic: stairs, every step the same height. Geometric: a rumor, each person tells two more.
Slope is a road sign: a 10% grade means 10 m up for every 100 m forward.
A circle is every point a goat can reach on a rope tied to a stake.
A delivery instruction: “3 km northeast” — how far and which way.
Walk halfway to a wall, again and again: you get as close as you like — the wall is the limit.
Izvod i primena: tangenta, min, max
A car’s speedometer: the derivative is how fast the distance is changing right now. At the top of a hill the road is flat for a moment — there the derivative is 0.
Filling a pool with a hose whose flow changes: the integral adds up all the little amounts.
Grain sizes in a riverbed sample: the mean is the typical grain, the deviation tells how mixed they are.
p: Currency exchange: convert everything to one currency (SI) before you add or compare.
Measuring a table with a ruler: the error says how much you trust the last digit.
Cruise control on the highway: the same distance every second.
Pressing the gas evenly: speed grows by the same amount each second.
A dropped phone. Without air, a hammer and a feather fall together — astronauts showed it on the Moon.
Push an empty and a full shopping cart equally hard: the heavy one accelerates less (F = ma).
Rubber soles on asphalt versus on ice — the same shoe, very different friction.
A stiletto heel versus an elephant foot: small area means huge pressure.
A phone battery: energy is what’s stored, power is how fast it drains.
Review week after the holidays — redo your error log.
Two independent movies: the stone moves sideways at constant speed and falls like a dropped stone at the same time.
In a turning car your body wants to go straight; the door pushes you toward the center.
A wheelchair ramp: a longer path, but a smaller force.
A truck and a bicycle at the same speed: the truck is far harder to stop.
A rollercoaster: height turns into speed and back again.
A tug of war on a rope that gets four times weaker when you double the distance.
Your ears hurt at the bottom of a pool; pumice floats because it’s less dense than water.
The sea stays cool in June and warm in September: water has a high specific heat.
A bag of chips puffs up on a mountain; a bicycle pump gets warm.
Heat flows from hot to cold like water flows downhill; no engine turns all heat into work.
A stadium wave: people only stand up and sit down, but the wave travels around.
Review week — redo your error log.
Like magnets: same charges push apart, opposite pull together, and both weaken fast with distance.
Water in pipes: voltage is pressure, current is flow, resistance is a narrow pipe.
Earth is a giant bar magnet; cooling lava freezes tiny compass needles in place — paleomagnetism.
A shopping cart rolling from asphalt onto grass turns because one wheel slows first — that’s refraction.
Popcorn: you can’t say which kernel pops next, but half pop in a set time — that’s how rocks are dated.
P: pushing a Slinky from one end. S: shaking a rope sideways. S can’t cross liquid, so the outer core is liquid.
The mantle is a pot of very thick soup slowly churning over millions of years; this convection is one of the forces that move the plates.
Rocks are stiff springs: they bend under stress, then snap — the snap is an earthquake.

c: For 2,000 years people believed everything was made of four elements: earth, water, air and fire. In his book The Sceptical Chymist, Boyle argued that a real element is something you can’t break down any further — the idea behind separating mixtures and finding pure substances.

Democritus guessed matter was made of tiny uncuttable pieces — “atomos”. 2,300 years later Rutherford’s team fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most went straight through, but a few bounced back — Rutherford said it was like firing a shell at tissue paper and having it come back. The atom was mostly empty, with a tiny heavy nucleus.

Bohr proposed that electrons can only sit on certain energy levels, like floors in a building — the start of electron configurations. During World War II, chemist George de Hevesy dissolved two colleagues’ gold Nobel medals in acid at Bohr’s institute to hide them from the Nazis. After the war the gold was recovered and the medals were recast.

Mendeleev arranged the 63 known elements by mass and properties, and boldly left gaps. He predicted the properties of three missing elements; gallium, scandium and germanium were found within 17 years and matched his predictions closely. Element 101, mendelevium, is named after him.

Pauling explained how and why atoms bond, and invented the electronegativity scale you use to decide whether a bond is ionic or covalent. He is the only person to win two unshared Nobel Prizes: Chemistry in 1954 and Peace in 1962.

Before Berzelius, chemists drew elements with alchemical pictures. He replaced them with letters taken from Latin names — that’s why sodium is Na (natrium), iron Fe (ferrum) and potassium K (kalium). He also measured atomic masses of almost all elements known at the time.

Old chemical names were poetic and useless: “oil of vitriol”, “butter of antimony”. These French chemists proposed naming compounds by what they’re made of — sulfates, oxides, chlorides. The system you’re learning in Serbian still follows their logic.

Lavoisier weighed everything before and after reactions in sealed vessels and showed that mass is never lost — the reason you balance equations. He was executed in 1794 during the French Revolution; the mathematician Lagrange said it took a moment to cut off that head, and a century might not produce another like it.

A pioneer of chemistry in Serbia. Lozanić taught chemistry in Belgrade for decades, was one of the founders of the Serbian Chemical Society, and became the first rector of the University of Belgrade in 1905 — the university you’re applying to.

Avogadro proposed that equal volumes of gases hold equal numbers of particles. Almost nobody listened for 50 years, until Stanislao Cannizzaro championed the idea at a chemistry congress in Karlsruhe in 1860. The famous number 6.022·10²³ was named after Avogadro much later.

Proust showed that a compound always contains its elements in the same mass ratio, wherever it comes from — natural copper carbonate and lab-made copper carbonate had the same composition. His long public debate with Claude-Louis Berthollet stayed polite, and Proust won.

Richter invented the word “stoichiometry” from Greek stoicheion (element) and metron (measure). He was obsessed with finding mathematical order in chemistry, and his tables of how much acid neutralizes how much base were early recipe ratios.

Nitroglycerin was so unstable that an explosion at the family factory killed Nobel’s younger brother. Nobel found that mixing it with kieselguhr — a soft sedimentary rock made of diatom shells — made it safe to handle: dynamite. His fortune funds the Nobel Prizes.

Gay-Lussac rode a hydrogen balloon to about 7,000 m to sample air and measure the atmosphere — a height record for decades. Back on the ground he found gases react in simple whole-number volume ratios, a key step toward molar volume.

Ostwald is often credited with introducing the word “mole” (from Molekül) and helped found physical chemistry as its own field. He won the 1909 Nobel Prize for work on catalysis, and later spent years developing a theory of colors.

Arrhenius’s PhD claimed that salts split into charged ions in water. His examiners gave it the lowest passing grade. Nineteen years later the same idea won him the Nobel Prize. In 1896 he was also the first to calculate how CO₂ could warm the Earth.

Sørensen worked at the Carlsberg brewery’s laboratory in Copenhagen, where acidity mattered for brewing and proteins. Writing tiny numbers like 0.0000001 was clumsy, so he introduced pH — a simple scale you now use for everything from soil to blood.

In the same year, the Danish chemist Johannes Brønsted and the English chemist Thomas Lowry, working separately, defined an acid as a proton donor and a base as a proton acceptor. That idea explains why some salt solutions turn acidic or basic.

Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper with brine-soaked cloth and got the first steady electric current — the voltaic pile. It runs on redox: one metal loses electrons, the other side gains them. The unit volt honors him.

They found how to push the N₂ + 3H₂ ⇌ 2NH₃ equilibrium toward ammonia with high pressure and a catalyst. Fertilizer from this process helps feed roughly half the world today. Haber’s legacy is also dark: he led Germany’s chemical weapons program in World War I.

Davy passed electric current through molten potash and saw tiny globules of a new metal burst into flame — potassium. His assistant recorded that Davy danced around the lab with joy. Within a year he had also isolated sodium, calcium and magnesium.

Father and son William Henry and Lawrence Bragg used X-rays to see how atoms are arranged in crystals, starting with salt. Lawrence later worked out the structures of silicate minerals. They shared the 1915 Nobel Prize; Lawrence was 25, still among the youngest winners ever.

Curie processed tonnes of pitchblende — the uranium mineral uraninite — by hand in a leaky shed to isolate about a tenth of a gram of pure radium chloride. She is the only person with Nobel Prizes in two different sciences, physics and chemistry. Persistence, one batch at a time.

People believed organic compounds could only be made by living things through a “vital force”. Wöhler made urea, a compound from urine, out of ammonium cyanate — an inorganic salt. Organic chemistry became plain chemistry of carbon.

Nobody could see how benzene’s six carbons fit together. Kekulé later said the answer came in a daydream of a snake biting its own tail — a ring. Whether the dream story is exactly true is debated, but the ring was right.

The Persian physician and alchemist al-Razi improved distillation and is often credited with early work on distilling alcohol. The word itself comes from Arabic al-kuḥl, a fine powder used as eye makeup; its meaning shifted over centuries to “the essence” of a liquid.

Liebig coined “aldehyde” from alcohol dehydrogenatus — alcohol with hydrogen removed, which is exactly how aldehydes form. He also invented the modern teaching lab, where students learn by doing experiments instead of only listening.

Chevreul showed that fats are made of fatty acids joined to glycerol, explained how soap forms and gave us better candles. He lived to 102 (1786–1889) and kept working into old age. A century later, Rosalind Franklin’s X-ray image known as Photo 51 showed that DNA, a biomolecule, is a helix. Watson and Crick used it, without her knowledge, to build their double-helix model; she died at 37, before the Nobel Prize was awarded.

After Mendeleev’s father died, his mother took him on a long journey from Siberia to Moscow and then St Petersburg to find a university that would accept him. She died soon after he was admitted. Exam season is hard — people before you have fought hard for a place too.

Hodgkin worked out the 3D structures of penicillin and vitamin B12 with X-rays (Nobel 1964), then spent 35 years on insulin until she solved it in 1969. Patience wins: rest, review, trust the work you’ve done.
m: The Indian mathematician Brahmagupta wrote rules for negative numbers using “fortunes” and “debts”: a debt minus zero is a debt, a debt times a debt is a fortune. Europe resisted negative numbers until the 1600s, calling them absurd.
Euclid’s method for finding the greatest common divisor — keep dividing and taking remainders — is one of the oldest algorithms still in daily use. Your phone uses relatives of it in encryption.

The Rhind papyrus (~1550 BC) shows Egyptians wrote fractions only as sums of 1/n pieces, like 2/5 = 1/3 + 1/15. Decimal fractions came to Europe through Simon Stevin, a Flemish engineer who argued that everyone should use them for money and measures.

“Percent” comes from Latin per centum, “for each hundred”. Emperor Augustus taxed goods sold at auction at 1/100 — the centesima rerum venalium. Merchants calculated with hundredths long before the % sign existed.

In The Sand Reckoner, Archimedes estimated how many grains of sand would fill the universe — about 10⁶³ in modern notation. Greek numbers couldn’t go that high, so he invented his own system of powers.
Working in Baghdad’s House of Wisdom, al-Khwarizmi wrote a book whose title included al-jabr — “restoring” — which became “algebra”. His own name, Latinized, became the word “algorithm”.

The triangle that gives (a + b)ⁿ is called Pascal’s triangle, but Chinese mathematician Yang Hui published it in 1261 and the Persian poet-mathematician Omar Khayyam knew it even earlier — centuries before Blaise Pascal.
Descartes started the habit of using x, y, z for unknowns and a, b, c for known values. A popular legend says his printer had more x’s left than other letters — probably untrue, but x stuck.

A Chinese textbook, the Nine Chapters on the Mathematical Art, solved systems of equations with counting rods laid out in a grid — essentially the elimination method you use, 2,000 years before Europeans named it after Gauss.
A clay tablet called Plimpton 322 lists Pythagorean triples like 3-4-5, more than 1,000 years before Pythagoras. Builders and surveyors used them to make right angles with knotted ropes.
Diophantus of Alexandria is called a father of algebra. A puzzle about his life says his boyhood was 1/6 of it, youth 1/12, then 1/7 more until marriage… Solve the equation and he lived to 84.

A famous story says Descartes, lying in bed, watched a fly on the ceiling and realized he could describe its position with two numbers. True or not, his coordinates let us draw equations as lines — every y = kx + n graph is his idea.
Viète, of the Vieta formulas, was a lawyer and royal codebreaker for King Henry IV of France. He cracked Spanish secret ciphers so well that Spain accused France of using sorcery.
Galileo showed that a thrown object follows a parabola — the graph of a quadratic function. Artillery gunners had been aiming with wrong ideas about curved-then-straight paths for centuries.

The Pythagoreans believed every length was a ratio of whole numbers. Legend says Hippasus proved √2 is not, and was drowned at sea for revealing it. The story is probably a myth, but irrational numbers really did shock Greek mathematics.

Bernoulli asked: if a bank paid 100% interest split into ever smaller periods, how much would 1 coin grow to in a year? The answer approached 2.718… — the number e, the base of natural exponential growth.

Napier, a Scottish laird, spent 20 years computing tables of logarithms so that multiplying huge numbers became adding. Astronomers loved it; Laplace later said logarithms doubled an astronomer’s working life by cutting the labor.

Hipparchus made the first trigonometric table to predict the positions of stars. The word “sine” comes from a translation mix-up: Sanskrit jya became Arabic jiba, misread as jaib (“fold, bay”) and translated into Latin as sinus.

Euler gave us the modern notation sin x, cos x and f(x), and wrote more mathematics than anyone in history. He lost the sight in both eyes and kept working, dictating results from memory — about half his work came after he went blind.

On the same day, the Sun was straight overhead in Syene but cast a shadow of about 7° in Alexandria. Using similar angles and the distance between the cities, Eratosthenes estimated Earth’s circumference remarkably close to the real value — early geodesy.

Archimedes proved a sphere has exactly 2/3 the volume of the cylinder around it, and asked for that picture on his tombstone. In 75 BC the Roman Cicero found the forgotten grave in Sicily by spotting the carved sphere and cylinder.

A Belgrade mathematician who studied in Paris and founded the Serbian school of mathematics. He was also a master river fisherman — alas means fisherman — and a violinist. His hydraulic machine for solving differential equations won a medal at the 1900 Paris World Exhibition.
The story goes that a teacher told 9-year-old Gauss’s class to add 1 to 100. Gauss paired 1 + 100, 2 + 99… 50 pairs of 101, and answered 5050 in seconds. That’s the arithmetic series formula.

Fermat, a lawyer who did math as a hobby, invented analytic geometry at the same time as Descartes. He scribbled in a book margin that he had a proof too large to fit — his “Last Theorem” waited more than 350 years until Andrew Wiles proved it in 1994.
Kepler spent years on Tycho Brahe’s observations of Mars before he accepted that orbits aren’t circles but ellipses — curves Apollonius of Perga had studied and named 1,800 years earlier.

Walking along a canal in Dublin, Hamilton suddenly saw how to multiply 3D quantities and carved the formula into Brougham Bridge with a knife. A plaque marks the spot; his quaternions led to the vectors used in physics and geology.

Zeno argued fast Achilles could never pass a tortoise, because he must first reach where it was, then where it moved, forever. It took until Cauchy and Weierstrass in the 1800s to define limits precisely and settle the puzzle.

Both invented calculus independently, then fought bitterly over who was first. The Royal Society’s official report favoring Newton was secretly written by Newton himself. We still use Leibniz’s notation, dy/dx.

Archimedes found the area of a parabolic segment by filling it with ever smaller triangles — the “method of exhaustion”, an early integral. He showed the area is exactly 4/3 of the largest triangle inside it.

Nightingale used statistics and her own “rose diagrams” to show that most soldiers in the Crimean War died from disease, not wounds. Her charts changed hospital sanitation, and she became the first woman member of the Royal Statistical Society.
p: Revolutionary France wanted units for everyone. Astronomers Delambre and Méchain spent seven years measuring the meridian from Dunkirk to Barcelona, and the metre was defined as one ten-millionth of the distance from the pole to the equator.
Without a telescope, Tycho measured star and planet positions more precisely than anyone before him. He also lost part of his nose in a sword duel over a math argument and wore a metal replacement.

Aristotle taught that a moving object needs a constant push to keep going. Galileo imagined a ball rolling on a perfectly smooth surface: it would roll forever. Uniform motion needs no force — the seed of Newton’s first law.
Galileo slowed down falling by rolling balls down gentle ramps and timing them with a water clock, weighing the water that flowed out. He found distance grows with the square of time — s = at²/2.

The story of Galileo dropping balls from the Leaning Tower of Pisa probably never happened. But in 1971 astronaut David Scott dropped a hammer and a feather on the Moon, on live TV — they landed together.
Newton’s Principia set out the three laws of motion and gravity. It almost wasn’t printed: the Royal Society had spent its budget on a book about fish, so Edmond Halley paid for the printing himself.
In his notebooks Leonardo sketched blocks being dragged and found friction doesn’t depend on contact area. His notes stayed unknown, and Guillaume Amontons rediscovered the same laws in 1699.

King Hiero suspected his gold crown contained silver. The story says Archimedes noticed water rising as he got into a bath, realized he could measure the crown’s volume and so its density — and ran through the streets shouting “Eureka!” Geologists still identify minerals by density.

Joule showed that work turns into heat in a fixed ratio by stirring water with falling weights. The story goes that on his honeymoon in the Alps he took thermometers to check whether waterfall water is warmer at the bottom. The unit of energy is the joule.

Born in Dubrovnik, Bošković proposed that matter is made of points with forces between them, attracting and repelling depending on distance — an idea that anticipated atomic theory. He also helped measure the shape of the Earth along a meridian in Italy.
Under house arrest by the Inquisition, old and nearly blind, Galileo wrote Two New Sciences. In it he showed that sideways and vertical motion are independent, so a projectile flies along a parabola.
The Dutch scientist derived the formula for centripetal acceleration, v²/r, and built the first accurate pendulum clock, keeping time to within seconds a day.

“Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth,” Archimedes is said to have boasted about levers. According to Plutarch, he pulled a fully loaded ship onto shore by himself using a system of pulleys.

Noether proved that every conservation law comes from a symmetry: momentum is conserved because physics works the same everywhere in space. Einstein called her a creative mathematical genius, yet for years she taught without pay because she was a woman.

As a ship’s doctor in the tropics, Mayer noticed sailors’ blood in their veins was brighter red — their bodies needed to burn less fuel to stay warm. That led him to the law of conservation of energy, though he struggled for years to be recognized.

The extremely shy Cavendish used a torsion balance with lead balls to measure gravity’s tiny pull between objects — “weighing the Earth”. He found Earth is about 5.5 times denser than water, much denser than surface rocks, so its interior must be heavy.

A famous demonstration attributed to Pascal: fix a long, thin tube into a closed barrel full of water and pour in just a few cups. The tall column raises the pressure so much the barrel bursts — pressure depends on depth, not amount.

In Glasgow, Black discovered that different substances need different amounts of heat to warm up (specific heat), and that melting ice absorbs heat without getting warmer (latent heat). His ideas helped his friend James Watt improve the steam engine.
Charles flew one of the first hydrogen balloons over Paris, before crowds of hundreds of thousands. His interest in how gases expand when heated gave us Charles’s law.

Carnot published only one book, on the limits of heat engines, which founded thermodynamics. He died of cholera at 36, and most of his papers were burned to prevent infection — the book was nearly forgotten until others rediscovered it.

Doppler predicted that a sound’s pitch changes when the source moves. In 1845 trumpeters played a steady note on a moving train while musicians on the platform judged the pitch — and it changed just as predicted.

Born in Titel in Vojvodina, Marić was one of the first women to study physics at the ETH in Zurich, where she met Albert Einstein and became his first wife. How much she contributed to his early work is still debated by historians.

Coulomb measured electric forces with a delicate torsion balance. Before that, as a military engineer, he studied how soil and retaining walls fail — the Mohr-Coulomb criterion is still used in rock mechanics and geotechnics today.

Ohm’s law was dismissed by many at first, and Ohm left his teaching post in Cologne; recognition came years later, with the Royal Society’s Copley Medal in 1841. Mihajlo Pupin, a shepherd boy from Idvor in Banat, invented “Pupin coils” that let telephone signals travel hundreds of kilometres. His autobiography won the Pulitzer Prize in 1924.

Walking in a Budapest park in 1882, Tesla suddenly saw how a rotating magnetic field could drive a motor, and sketched it in the sand. His alternating-current system powers the world, the unit of magnetic field is the tesla, and his ashes rest in the Nikola Tesla Museum in Belgrade.

In his Book of Optics, the Arab scholar Ibn al-Haytham showed that we see because light enters the eye, and studied reflection, refraction and the camera obscura. He insisted on testing ideas with experiments — an early form of the scientific method.

Becquerel left uranium salts on a wrapped photographic plate in a drawer and found it fogged anyway — radioactivity. In Paris in 1938, the Serbian scientist Pavle Savić and Irène Joliot-Curie found an unexpected lanthanum-like substance in uranium hit by neutrons, a step toward the discovery of nuclear fission.

Studying records of an earthquake in the Kupa valley in Croatia, Mohorovičić saw two sets of seismic waves arriving at different times. He concluded there is a boundary between crust and mantle — today called the Moho. In 1936 Danish seismologist Inge Lehmann found Earth’s solid inner core the same way.

A Belgrade professor who calculated, by hand, how changes in Earth’s orbit change the sunlight reaching it — and so cause ice ages. Much of the work was done while he was interned in Budapest during World War I. In 1976 ocean sediment cores confirmed his “Milanković cycles”; craters on the Moon and Mars carry his name.

Hooke found his law around 1660 and announced it in 1676 as an anagram, ceiiinosssttuv, to claim priority without revealing it: ut tensio, sic vis — “as the extension, so the force.” He also argued that fossils are remains of real living things. Centuries later Alfred Wegener argued that continents drift apart — the coasts of Africa and South America fit like puzzle pieces. Most geologists laughed; in the 1960s plate tectonics proved him right.

c: Which of these is a mixture: distilled water, air, NaCl, O₂?
Air — a mixture of N₂, O₂, Ar, CO₂… The others are pure substances.
How would you separate sand from table salt?
Dissolve in water → filter (sand stays on the filter) → evaporate the water (salt remains).

Element Z = 19: which group and period? Name it.
Which is more metallic, Na or Mg? Why?
Na — it’s further left in the same period and gives away its one electron more easily.
Bond type in HCl, KBr and Fe?

4Al + 3O₂ → 2Al₂O₃ (6 O atoms on each side, then 4 Al).

Decomposition (analiza) — heating limestone to make quicklime.
Molar mass of H₂SO₄ (H 1, S 32, O 16)?
How many moles are in 4.4 g CO₂?
How many molecules are in 0.5 mol H₂O?
Mass percent of Fe in Fe₂O₃ (Fe 56, O 16)?
A compound is 40% C, 6.7% H, 53.3% O. Empirical formula?
How many grams of CaO come from 50 g CaCO₃?
CaCO₃ → CaO + CO₂. n = 50/100 = 0.5 mol → 0.5 · 56 = 28 g CaO.
How many grams of O₂ are needed to burn 12 g of carbon?
C + O₂ → CO₂. n(C) = 1 mol → n(O₂) = 1 mol → 32 g.
4 g H₂ react with 16 g O₂. Which is limiting? Mass of water?
n(H₂) = 2, n(O₂) = 0.5. 2H₂ + O₂: 0.5 mol O₂ needs only 1 mol H₂ → O₂ limits. Water: 1 mol = 18 g.
100 g of limestone is 80% CaCO₃. Volume of CO₂ (STP) with excess HCl?
80 g CaCO₃ = 0.8 mol → 0.8 mol CO₂ · 22.4 = 17.92 L.

read: Muzej Nikole Tesle, Krunska 51, Beograd
Tesla’s personal items, working models of his inventions, and the urn with his ashes. A good weekend break.
Mihajlo Pupin — Sa pašnjaka do naučenjaka
Pupin’s autobiography (From Immigrant to Inventor), Pulitzer Prize 1924. From shepherd boy in Idvor to Columbia professor.
Milutin Milanković — Kroz vasionu i vekove
Popular science in Serbian, written as letters, about the history of astronomy and science.
Sam Kean — The Disappearing Spoon
Short, funny stories behind the elements of the periodic table. Check for a Serbian edition.
Primo Levi — Periodni sistem (The Periodic Table)
A chemist’s life told through 21 elements.
Bill Bryson — A Short History of Nearly Everything
The story of science and the people behind it, including a lot of geology. Check for a Serbian edition.
BBC — Chemistry: A Volatile History
Three-part documentary by physicist Jim Al-Khalili on how the elements were discovered.
BBC — The Story of Maths
Four-part documentary by Marcus du Sautoy, from Egypt and Babylon to modern mathematics.
Cosmos: A Spacetime Odyssey (2014)
13 episodes with Neil deGrasse Tyson, with animated stories of scientists like Newton, Faraday and Clair Patterson, who measured Earth’s age.
Simon Singh — Fermat’s Last Theorem
A hunt of more than 350 years for one proof, told like a detective story.
